No.

Think of it like this.

An R1 appears once on a sheet. An R2 appears twice.

If we had 50 R2s and 50 R1s, a sheet would have:

100 R2s
50 R1s

Hence, an R1 would be worth roughly two R2s, because you'd be twice as
likely to get any given R2 as any given R1.

However, consider a situation with 50 R2 and 1 R1:

100 R2s
1 R1

Hence, an R1 would be much more valuable in this scenario. If you only
have 1 rare per booster, you're only likely to get it in 1 in every 101
boosters - roughly a 1% chance.

If you alter the numbers to the current situation, you get trades like
those suggested.

But it isn't, you see. If there were 25 R2s and 25 R1s, yes, that would
be the case.

But there are 46 R2s and only 8 R1s, all competing for the single
R slot in the booster. That means, in a given booster, you're six
times more likely to pull a R2 than a R1:

1 Rare Slot: 46/54 chance of R2, 8/54 chance of R1

Expected value of a rare pull: 0.148(periodic), or 14.814% of a R1,
85.185% of a R2.

How did I get 0.148? I got it by calculating the odds of drawing
an R2: 46/54, which is equal to 23/27. 23/27 is 0.851(periodic),
so the odds of R1 must be 1-(P[R2]), or 14.814(periodic).

(Tangent: For Uncommons/Commons, things get trickier as there's
more than one slot; I only have the math to get the odds of
at least one U1/C1 per so many packs, so those numbers are a little
wafflier since I didn't do math for pulling _exactly one_ U1/C1. I might
be able to get my Abomination for slightly fewer than 729 Canopic Jars).

You should expect to pull one R1 every 6.75 packs exactly, or
(normalized) 4 every 27 packs.

(tangent2: I pulled 5 R1s out of 72 packs, short 5 and 2/3rds R1s.
arrgh. OTOH, I bought 10 packs over the weekend, which gave up 3
R1s. And I pulled one R1 out of the 2 boosters I got at the Pre-Release.
So that makes 9 R1s in 84 packs, with expected yield 12.44 R1s. I don't
know where the missing 3.444 R1s got to, but it's the vagaries of the
Holy Card Sorter. I blame Xian, who is, in all likelihood, pulling 3 and
4 Lupine Assaults and Abominations out of each booster and cackling madly.)

That means that for 4 R1s, you have pulled 23 R2s. At 6x4=24, a ratio
of 6 R2s for an R1 is about right if you're operating on scarcity
value alone. Personally, I wouldn't give up 6 Shroud Masteries for
one Mythic Form, but that's how the numbers shake out on a strictly
scarcity analysis, which is important for set collectors, I suppose.

Aaron wrote:
> Maybe it doesn't matter...but Jyhad included Rares and rare2's. And
> you don't see people trading 5 "Behind You!"(R2) for 1 "Betrayer"(R1)

You're not making a critical distinction. There's a huge difference
between having lots of R1s and a few R2s vs. lots of R2s and a few R1s.

If there's lots of R1s, people buy product as if they have to cover lots
of R1 rare cards they'll need and set their expectation of price vs.
payoff accordingly. That is, they're basically buying a singe R1 in
every pack (and get annoyed if it's a bad/mediocre R2 but go on) and
gauge whether the pack price is worth what they get from that expectation.
And they can easily trade the R1s they don't want for R1s they do.
Basically, if you don't get any particular R1 in your pack, it doesn't
matter because you'll usually get another R1.

When you have a few R1s amongst many R2s, that really screws a lot of
things up. People kind of have to buy packs with the expectation of
getting R2s. It's very hard to predict when those occasional R1s will
come up or how many you'll get, even if you buy lots and lots of packs.
They can be extremely hard to trade for depending on who you know to
trade with and whether those people draw what you want in their packs.
Everything gets real awkward since players have a very difficult time
figuring out what the true trade or sales volume of an R1 actually is
Dealers either sell out of them immediately or put outrageous prices on
them. Or both.

This is a bad thing. I hope White Wolf avoids this in the future. It's
not worth it.

Fred

It depends on what you mean by "too many rares". If you replace a 100 card
rare sheet which has 8 R1s and 46 X 2 = 92 R2s (I'm assuming that's how it's
been done) with 100 R1s and still include the 10 other cards and charge $2.75
per pack for it, then perhaps. But it wouldn't be much worse since no card
is any more rare than R1. And at least if you didn't draw an Abomination (for
instance) you'd draw any one of 99 other R1s that were as rare as an Abomination
and hence likely to be tradable for an Abomination (exact card utility not
withstanding). This way, you'll likely get an R2 instead, which is automatically
somewhat less valuable.

In any event, any kind of scheme that makes the existing R1s more common
per pack (that is, allows you to have a better chance of drawing in a given
pack) would be a distinct improvement.

> How would you recommend redistributing the 162 FN booster pack cards, for instance?

The obvious answer would be to print a card sheet with 54 cards on it
and make them all R1s. If you could do anything you liked. If the problem
is that you're stuck (due to the process of the manufacturer you're using)
with 100-card card sheets then it would have been a vast improvement to print
50 R2s and move the other 4 into uncommon card sheets. Printing U1s in an
expansion that has rarer R2s is not a problem at all since U1s aren't the most
rare card.

> guess I should have predicted it. No matter how things are done,
> there'll be someone out there that will complain about it.

Well, that's an eternal truth. :-)

My complaints are based on my experience with collectible card games. Some people
love the concept of super-rares. Over time, though, I've found that ultra rare
cards, unless utter wallpaper or so specialized that most people don't care
about them, tend to make the player population somewhat edgy. If a card seems like
it can be abused at all, the calls to ban it will be much more emotional. Poorer
players feel left out when someone pulls out a deck that has a half-dozen of the
super-rares. Stuff like that.

Don't get me wrong. These R1s are not likely to be any worse then some of the Sabbat
rares were unless they prove highly useful in large numbers. Still, I don't think
the rarity of The Sabbat rares - especially after the supply of Sabbat dried up - was
a good thing, either.

Fred

I'm not sure why you say that. It's not very clear what R1 is worth vs. and
R2 even if the play value is identical. The fact that they printed two R2s
for every R1 is somewhat coincidental to trade value. One plus one doesn't
really equal two in this sense.

For example, if they print 10,000 "Alpha" cards ("Alpha" being the theoretical
name of a specific card) and 20,000 "Beta" cards because Alphas are R1s and
Betas are R2 and they printed enough packs to use the cards from 10,000 rare
card sheets, it's anyone's guess how many of these cards will be available for
play. If there are 5,000 collectors out there each wanting to sock away one
each of every card - including one Alpha and one Beta - and if they succeed at
doing so, 5,000 Alphas and 15,000 Betas remain available for card players to
play with. This translates into a three-to-one ration instead of a two-to-one.
Of course, 5,000 sets of cards in relation to 10,000 of a given R1 is a huge
number and I wouldn't expect anything like that. I'm just showing how the
unpredictable the effect of peoples' aggregate buying behaviors is on the trade
value of a card.

And play value. It's one thing to state that two cards have the same play value
but what does that mean? If they're two cards like Tasha Morgan and J.R. Simmons,
Esq., people will usually use a small number of them and don't care all that much
if they have two Tashas and no J.R. Simmons instead of one of each. Or can just
skip the J.R. Simmons if they don't have one and use something else. But if they're
two cards that do nothing by themselves and are kick-ass together as a combo, it
matters a lot more that you actually have one of each and aren't missing either
card.

The point is that it's real tricky to what an R1 is worth in comparison to an R2,
just as it's tricky to compare the trade value of uncommons to rares. It may be
more or less than the 2-1 ratio of the number of cards that got printed. My experience
is that it's likely to be more than 2-1 just as you can seldom trade three average
uncommons for an average rare in most CCG expansions that are printed up in 3-1
uncommon/rare ratios.

> Also, having a BOATLOAD of commons, you can likely get someone who
> bought far fewer cards, but has one copy of an R1 you want to trade for,
> trading away what is purely *excess* cards for you.

Well, I've never been able to do that but then I've never been much of trader.
But usually, the commons people are willing to take in exchange for rarer cards
are *exactly* the few issues of common cards you can actually use in large number;
Wakes, Forced Awakenings, Majesties and like that. Which is not surprising.
